title: NIH Grant Awards and Funding Opportunity Notices Fell, Analysts Say
date_basis: March 15, 2026 is the dated snapshot for Ginexi's notice analysis; VPM separately reports Berg's early-2026 award count.
description_short: Analysts report fewer NIH grants and delayed funding notices; the counts measure different things.
description_medium: An NPR report quoted Jeremy Berg’s analysis that NIH had issued about 2,300 new grants in early 2026, roughly 66% fewer than in the comparable period a year earlier. It also reported Elizabeth Ginexi’s finding that 205 of 336 open forecasts were past their promised posting dates. Separately, Ginexi’s Chronicle analysis counted 756 funding-opportunity notices in 2024, 120 in 2025 and 14 by March 15, 2026. Awards and notices are different measures; these attributed counts do not establish covert intent or a shift to larger grants.
description_long: A May 2026 NPR report carried by VPM quoted former NIH official Jeremy Berg’s analysis that the National Institutes of Health had issued roughly 2,300 new grants in the first few months of 2026, about 66% fewer than in the comparable period a year earlier. The report also quoted former NIH program officer Elizabeth Ginexi, whose review found that 205 of 336 NIH funding forecasts still listed as open were past their promised posting dates without a full announcement. Separately, Ginexi’s Chronicle of Higher Education analysis counted 756 NIH funding-opportunity notices posted in 2024, 120 in 2025 and 14 by March 15, 2026; she said 61 of 75 notices forecast for 2026 had not yet been published. These figures describe distinct measures: grants issued, delayed forecasts and posted notices. They document a sharp slowdown and delays as reported by named analysts, but do not prove that NIH acted covertly, deliberately shifted to larger awards, or concealed an intact budget. VPM also reports the administration’s explanation for funding delays; that explanation does not resolve the cause of each count. The original headline’s claim of covert manipulation is unsupported.

sources.title: VPM/NPR, Researchers say the Trump administration is finding new ways to punish science
sources.supports: Reports Berg's roughly 2,300 NIH awards and 66% year-over-year decline in the first months of 2026; attributes Ginexi's finding that 205 of 336 open forecasts were overdue; includes HHS's stated explanation for delays.

sources.title: The Chronicle of Higher Education, Why Is the NIH Abandoning Science?
sources.supports: Ginexi's Grants.gov analysis of NIH funding-opportunity notices: 756 in 2024, 120 in 2025, 14 by March 15, 2026, and 61 of 75 forecast 2026 notices not yet published.

notes: The prior draft conflated grants awarded with funding-opportunity notices and overstated intent. Keep the separate VPM/NPR and Chronicle counts attributed to their analysts; source_triage was needs_correction, not accepted_source.

title: FEC Lacks a Voting Quorum as Enforcement Backlog Reaches at Least 195 Matters
date_basis: The reviewed sources do not establish the precise date the Commission first fell below quorum; the exact start date remains unresolved.
description_short: FEC quorum loss limited commission votes; NOTUS reported at least 195 pending enforcement matters in March 2026.
description_medium: Ellen Weintraub disputed Trump’s January 2025 attempt to remove her from the FEC. After later commissioner departures, the Commission lacked the four affirmative votes required for certain actions. NOTUS reported at least 195 pending enforcement matters in early March 2026, citing Chair Shana Broussard. The reports support a voting and enforcement backlog, not the claim that the FEC could take no action of any kind or lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump’s term; the exact onset is not established here.
description_long: President Donald Trump sent Federal Election Commission Chair Ellen Weintraub a letter purporting to remove her in January 2025; she disputed the legality of the move. Subsequent commissioner departures left the Commission without the four affirmative votes required for certain commission actions. The FEC’s announcement about Commissioner Allen Dickerson’s departure documents a later vacancy, while NOTUS reported in early March 2026 that at least 195 enforcement matters were pending, citing Chair Shana Broussard. Those facts support a serious constraint on commission-level enforcement decisions and a reported backlog. They do not establish that the agency could take no action of any kind, that every pending matter was caused by the quorum loss, or that the Commission lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of the president’s term. The cited material does not give a sufficiently documented start date for the period without quorum, so this correction leaves the precise date unresolved rather than repeating May 1, 2025 as settled. It also does not establish a zero-dollar fine total or the timing of later nominations. The entry is limited to the disputed removal, later vacancies, and reported March 2026 backlog.

title: Social Security Administration Announces Plan to Reduce Workforce from About 57,000 to 50,000
description_short: SSA set a 50,000-employee target, down from about 57,000, while anticipating many voluntary departures.
description_medium: On February 28, 2025, the Social Security Administration announced a target to reduce staffing from roughly 57,000 employees to 50,000 while reorganizing its regional and headquarters structure. SSA said it expected many departures through retirement, deferred resignation and voluntary separation, while leaving open possible reductions in force. The release states a workforce plan; it does not show that thousands had already been involuntarily fired or establish later service effects.
description_long: On February 28, 2025, the Social Security Administration announced a plan to reduce its workforce from roughly 57,000 employees to 50,000 and reorganize its regional and headquarters structure. The stated target was a reduction of about 7,000 positions. SSA said it expected much of the reduction to come through retirement, deferred resignation and voluntary separation incentives, while also allowing that reductions in force could be used. The agency’s release described a workforce target and planned changes; it did not say that DOGE itself ordered or carried out thousands of involuntary terminations. A staffing target and an expectation of voluntary departures do not establish how many employees ultimately left, how many positions were eliminated through layoffs, or what happened to local service capacity. Those outcomes require later agency records or independent reporting. The original July 2025 headline also misdates the announcement: the cited SSA release is dated February 28. This entry therefore reports the announced target and the agency’s stated approach without presenting proposed reductions as completed firings or asserting unmeasured operational consequences.

sources.title: Social Security Administration, Social Security Administration Announces Agency Restructuring
sources.supports: Official February 28, 2025 announcement of the approximate 57,000-to-50,000 staffing target and expected use of retirement and voluntary separation, with possible RIF actions.

notes: The cited release documents an announced target, not completed layoffs or a measured service impact.

title: Trump Removes NLRB Member and Two EEOC Commissioners, Leaving Both Bodies Without Quorums
description_short: Trump removed one NLRB member and two EEOC commissioners; both agencies lost a quorum for certain board-level decisions.
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, President Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and EEOC commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels. Reuters reported that vacancies left both bodies without a quorum for specified board- or commission-level decisions. The reports document a constraint on formal board action, not the firing of every member or the end of every agency function; they do not establish that all investigations or regional enforcement stopped.
description_long: On January 27, 2025, President Donald Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels. Reuters reported that existing vacancies combined with these removals left both agencies without the quorum needed for specified board- or commission-level decisions. The NLRB’s official biography confirms that Wilcox’s term was due to end in 2028 and says Trump removed her before its expiration. The two agencies have different responsibilities: the NLRB handles labor relations and unfair labor practice matters, while the EEOC addresses employment discrimination. Losing a quorum constrained formal collective decisions, but the cited reports do not show that every member was fired, that every investigation stopped, or that regional enforcement work ceased. Legal challenges over the removals followed. This narrower account corrects the original claim that Trump fired all members and paralyzed both agencies, while retaining the documented institutional consequence: each body lacked a quorum for actions requiring a vote of the full board or commission.

sources.supports: Reports Wilcox's January 27 removal and its effect on the NLRB's quorum and decision-making.

title: DOGE Sought IRS Data Access; Officials Agreed to Limit Access to Anonymized Data
description_short: Reports say DOGE sought IRS data access, then agreed to read-only access to anonymized data rather than individual returns.
description_medium: In February 2025, DOGE personnel sought access to IRS systems during the administration’s government-wide review. The Washington Post reported that Treasury and White House officials later agreed to limit the IRS DOGE representative to read-only, anonymized data and bar access to personal taxpayer information. These reports document an access request and negotiated restrictions; they do not show that DOGE inspected tax returns belonging to political opponents, donors or journalists.
description_long: In February 2025, Department of Government Efficiency personnel sought access to sensitive Internal Revenue Service systems as part of the administration’s government-wide review. The Washington Post reported the initial request on February 16 and, four days later, reported an agreement by Treasury and White House officials to prohibit access to personal taxpayer data and limit the DOGE representative’s access to read-only, anonymized data. That sequence matters: the request raised legitimate concerns because tax records contain highly sensitive personal and financial information, but a request followed by a negotiated access limit is not evidence that DOGE inspected identifiable returns. The supplied reports do not document DOGE viewing individual returns belonging to political opponents, donors or journalists. The supported account concerns the proposed access, privacy safeguards and questions about oversight, not a demonstrated political search of taxpayer files. Any claim about data actually queried or safeguards breached would require separate records showing what information was available and how it was used. This correction keeps the reported access dispute while removing the unsupported claim that DOGE accessed political opponents’ tax records.
